meta.title: Vimdow — Vim-style window management for macOS
meta.description: Move, resize, snap, and switch macOS windows from the keyboard with Vim's hjkl, counts, and undo. Free and open source.

hero.lead: Vimdow is a keyboard-driven window manager for macOS. Press one shortcut to enter command mode, then move, resize, snap, and switch windows with h, j, k, l, counts, and the other Vim habits already in your fingers. The mouse stays where it is.
hero.copyFailed: Select the command and copy it manually.

demo.aria: Animated demo: in command mode, Vim keys move a window, widen it, center it, undo that, and snap it to the left half. A second window is then picked by number and snapped to the right half.
demo.videoUnsupported: Your browser cannot play this video.

steps.right: l moves the window right, one step per press.
steps.down: 12j moves it down twelve steps at once.
steps.grow: Option–l widens it, keeping the top-left corner in place.
steps.center: zz centers it on the display.
steps.half: Control–W, then H, fills the left half.
steps.switch: Q numbers the windows; 2 switches to the second one and leaves command mode.
steps.tile: Back in command mode, Control–W, then L, fills the right half with it.

why.title: Why Vimdow
why.p1: Vimdow was written by someone who has used Vim since 1998 and would rather not reach for the mouse. Almost everything on a Mac could be done from the keyboard except managing windows: nudging one a few points, or sending it to another display, always meant leaving the home row.
why.p2: The first version, in 2013, was a small Objective-C app that fixed exactly that for one user. Instead of new shortcuts to learn, it mapped window operations onto the Vim vocabulary: hjkl to move, a count to repeat, 0 and $ for the edges, gg and G for the top and bottom, zz to center, u to undo, / to search. In 2026 it was rewritten in Swift 6 with a tested command engine.
why.p3: Vimdow is modal, like Vim. It is not a tiling window manager and does not arrange windows for you; it makes arranging them yourself fast. It is one person's preference, published for anyone whose hands have the same habits.

enter.title: Enter command mode
enter.text_html: Press <kbd>⌃</kbd><kbd>⌥</kbd><kbd>A</kbd> and release. Until you leave, keys go to Vimdow instead of the frontmost app.

move.title: Move and resize
move.text_html: <kbd>h</kbd> <kbd>j</kbd> <kbd>k</kbd> <kbd>l</kbd> move the focused window by a configurable step. Type a count to repeat, hold a key to glide, and add Option or Shift to resize.

leave.title: Leave
leave.text_html: Press <kbd>esc</kbd> or <kbd>.</kbd> to return to normal mode. Your typing goes back to the app.

move.title: Move and resize with counts
move.text: Steps are configurable, keys repeat while held, and every change glides into place. 12j moves twelve steps; Option and Shift resize from opposite corners.

snap.title: Snap and tile
snap.text: 0, $, gg, G, and zz put a window at an edge or the center, keeping its size. Control–W followed by H, J, K, or L fills half the display; followed by O, all of it.

undo.title: Undo and redo, per window
undo.text: u and Control–R step through each window's own history of moves, resizes, snaps, and display changes, even if you have since dragged it by hand.

displays.title: Displays that remember
displays.text: Control–Option–K or L sends a window to the next display. Bring it back and it lands exactly where it was.

switch.title: Switch without hunting
switch.text: Q shows large white numbers in translucent black badges at window centers. Overlapping badges spread out; selection cancels after three seconds without keyboard input. Type a digit to focus a window, or use / to search and n and N to cycle matches.

settings.title: Yours to tune
settings.text: Set separate move and resize steps, choose whether resizing stops at display edges, turn the glide off, and rebind the seven global shortcuts.

marks.title: Switch between your chosen windows
marks.text: Press M in command mode to mark a window, then Control–Option–[ for the previous mark or Control–Option–] for the next. Cycle in registration order, wrapping at either end. The destination pulses twice, for 0.18 seconds each. Marks last until Vimdow quits; hidden windows rejoin when visible.

cheat.title: Command mode at a glance
cheat.intro: Enter with Control–Option–A (the default). Digits typed before a command repeat it. Two keys shown together are pressed one after the other.
cheat.note: Keys are bound to physical ANSI positions, so they stay in the same place on JIS, Korean, and other layouts.

rows.move: Move left, down, up, right by one step
rows.resizeTL: Resize, keeping the top-left corner fixed
rows.resizeBR: Resize, keeping the bottom-right corner fixed
rows.undo: Undo / redo the focused window's last change
rows.edges: Move to the left / right edge of the display
rows.topBottom: Move to the top / bottom edge
rows.halves: Fill the left / bottom / top / right half
rows.numbered: Focus a numbered window; Q pages; three seconds idle cancels
rows.search: Search by application name; next / previous match
rows.mark: Mark / unmark the focused window and exit command mode
rows.markedCycle: Cycle marked windows, also available in normal mode

different.question: How is Vimdow different from Rectangle or a tiling window manager?
different.answer: Rectangle and similar apps give each layout its own global shortcut, and tiling window managers such as yabai and AeroSpace arrange windows for you. Vimdow does neither. One shortcut enters command mode, where a handful of Vim keys move, resize, snap, and undo, and no window moves until you ask.

vim.question: Do I need to know Vim?
vim.answer: No. Four keys cover most of it: h, j, k, and l move a window left, down, up, and right. Counts, gg, zz, and the rest are there when you want them, and the cheat sheet above lists every key.

layouts.question: Does it work with Korean, Japanese, and other keyboard layouts?
layouts.answer: Yes. Command-mode keys are bound to physical key positions rather than characters, so h, j, k, and l work whatever input source is active. Searching by app name accepts Korean, Japanese, and other input methods.

shortcuts.question: Can I change the shortcuts?
shortcuts.answer: You can rebind or clear the seven global shortcuts in Settings, including Control–Option–A for command mode and Control–Option–[ and Control–Option–] for previous and next marked windows. Keys inside command mode are fixed, so they always mean the same thing.

apps.question: Does it work with every app?
apps.answer: It works with any app whose windows macOS lets other apps move, which is nearly all of them. When an app refuses a move or resize, for example a window with a fixed size, Vimdow beeps instead of forcing it.

update.question: How do I update Vimdow?
update.answer: Quit Vimdow, then download the latest Vimdow.zip and replace the app in Applications. If installed with Homebrew, run brew update and brew upgrade --cask vimdow. Settings stay; window marks reset on restart. Vimdow never checks for updates itself.

get.title: Get Vimdow
get.intro: Vimdow 1.1.0 supports macOS 14 or later, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. The app is signed with Developer ID and notarized by Apple.
get.move: Move Vimdow.app from the downloaded zip to Applications.
get.allow: Open it, then allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility.
get.accessibilityText: macOS requires it for any app that moves another app's windows. Vimdow uses it for that and nothing else: no network access, no analytics, nothing leaves your Mac.

footer.credits_html: Jang Ho Hwang has been building Vimdow since 2013. Yoo Yong-Ha wrote its first command window the same year. Global shortcuts use the KeyboardShortcuts library (MIT License).
footer.privacy: This site sets no cookies and runs no analytics.
